title: Where Jansenius differs from Molina: natural affections or heaven-sent
source_text: CXII. Verum in eo differt a Molina, quod affectus istiusmodi, secundum Molinae doctrinam, mere naturaliter in voluntate oriuntur, posita mentis illuminatione: nec aliud praestat Deus, quam quod affectibus illis peculiari influxu se ingerit, eosque reddit supernaturales. Juxta Jansenium vero, posita quacunque mentis illuminatione, affectus isti in hominis corrupti voluntate per naturam non exurgunt, sed necesse est illos totos coelitus immitti, non simpliciter quadam divina motione acui, & intendi, ut fiant supernaturales.
pass_a_gloss: CXII. But he differs from Molina in this, that affections of this kind, according to Molina's doctrine, arise merely naturally in the will, illumination of the mind being posited: nor does God do anything else, than that he thrusts himself into those affections by a peculiar influx, and renders them supernatural. But according to Jansenius, any illumination of the mind whatever being posited, those affections do not rise up by nature in the will of corrupt man, but it is necessary that they be sent in wholly from heaven, not simply sharpened & intensified by some divine motion, that they may become supernatural.
pass_b_english: Thesis CXII. He differs from Molina, however, in this. On Molina's doctrine such affections arise in the will purely by nature once the mind is illuminated, and God does no more than thrust himself into them by a special influence and make them supernatural.

On Jansenius's view, whatever illumination of the mind is given, these affections do not rise by nature in the will of fallen man. They must be sent into it wholly from heaven, and not merely sharpened and heightened by some divine motion so as to become supernatural.

lemmas.gloss: arise merely naturally in the will
thrusts himself in by a peculiar influx
that they be sent in wholly from heaven

choices.why: Jansenius's heavenly delight is infused whole, not a natural affection heightened, as in Molina.
